tagline.text: The old stone house in Maragondon where the Katipunan leader stood trial before a military court

location.label: Location
location.text: Col. C. Riel Street, Maragondon town proper, Cavite

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (free admission; rough day-trip total including transport and meals)

children.text: The Bonifacio Trial House in Maragondon, Cavite is a two-story stone house built in 1889, where Andres Bonifacio and his brother stood trial before a military court in 1897. It now operates as an NHCP museum with a life-size trial diorama and exhibits on the revolution.

The Bonifacio Trial House sits in the town proper of Maragondon, Cavite. According to tradition, Andres Bonifacio, leader of the Katipunan secret society that led the Philippine Revolution, was tried here by a military court in May 1897. Wikipedia describes the house as built in 1889, a two-story bahay na bato of stone, brick, and wood. The owner's name appears slightly differently on signs and in sources, for example Roderico Reyes or Teodorico Reyes.

Here is the background. After the Tejeros Convention in Cavite on March 22, 1897, Bonifacio fell out with Emilio Aguinaldo's faction, was arrested in Indang, and was brought to Maragondon with his younger brother Procopio. The two were charged with treason and sedition on May 5, sentenced to death the next day, and are said to have been executed in the mountains near Maragondon on May 10. The old 1948 marker says a military court headed by Brigadier General Mariano Noriel sat here and that Bonifacio was shot on Mount Buntis, but the exact place and circumstances of the execution are still debated.

The house was declared a National Historical Landmark by the National Historical Institute (now the NHCP) on June 4, 1997, and carries an English marker from 1948 and a Filipino marker from 2000. It is government-owned and now serves as the NHCP-run
Museo ng Paglilitis ni Andres Bonifacio

(Bonifacio Trial Museum). The museum opened on November 28, 2014, and recreates the trial with life-size dioramas. It is small and an hour or two is enough, but standing in a quiet town in southwestern Cavite at a dark moment of revolutionary history stays with you.

A little background on the man makes the exhibits easier to read. Andres Bonifacio was born in Tondo, Manila, on November 30, 1863, founded the Katipunan (KKK) in July 1892 to prepare an armed revolution against Spanish colonial rule, and became its leader when the revolution began in August 1896. That he was tried and died after a conflict within the revolutionary camp itself is what gives this house its weight. The museum lets you follow this story through timelines and panels, so read them slowly in order. The explanations are clear enough that the site is even recommended as a school field-trip destination.

The centerpiece of the museum is a life-size diorama that recreates the trial of the Bonifacio brothers. After a renovation it is reported to use light and sound together. Watching the introductory video first helps you understand the scene in context.

This two-story stone house follows the bahay na bato style, with stone and brick below and mostly timber above. One blog names the original staircase as the only part of the house that survives in its original form. Take your time looking at the stairs, the floorboards, and how the windows are built.

Display panels explain events in order, from the founding of the Katipunan to Bonifacio's execution. Revolution-era artifacts, Katipunan flags, paintings, a bust, and panels on Maragondon's local history and the KKK are reported to be on the second floor. Exhibits are rearranged from time to time, so check on site.

One space is devoted to Gregoria de Jesus, Bonifacio's wife. The NHCP has held a special exhibition on women of the Katipunan in the gallery here. It is a chance to see the role of women in the revolution.

The museum covers not only Bonifacio but also his family, including his brother Procopio. The NHCP has held talks and exhibits on the brothers' roles. Check NHCP announcements for events during your visit.

In front of the house you will find the 1948 English marker and the 2000 Filipino marker. The markers themselves are records that have accumulated over time since the landmark designation, and reading them before you go in changes how you see the exhibits.

The NHCP has held a wreath-laying around May 10, the anniversary of the execution, and an event on November 30, Bonifacio's birthday. Visiting near those dates may give you a chance to hear commentary in a commemorative atmosphere. Programs change every year, so check ahead.

Maragondon is a small town known for bamboo crafts, old houses, and a church. The trial house is described as a few blocks from the town hall, so the town is easy to explore on foot. The local church is the Our Lady of the Assumption Parish Church.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: Half a day at the museum and in town

children.text: Take a bus toward Ternate or Maragondon from Manila (such as PITx). Check bus companies and schedules at the terminal.
Get off in Maragondon and walk toward the town hall to reach the trial house on Col. C. Riel Street.
Watch the introductory video, then take your time through the diorama and the second-floor exhibits. The museum is closed on Mondays, so avoid that day.
Take photos of the marker in front of the house and the building's exterior.
Have lunch at a local eatery in town and stroll toward the Maragondon church.
Check the return bus times and leave before dark.

Some stretches may have infrequent public transport, so leave generous time for the trip home. This schedule is only one example. Outside museum time, it helps to leave breathing room by having a snack in town or resting in front of the church. On rainy days, spend more time inside and shorten the town stroll.
Start at Aguinaldo Shrine in Kawit, the stage of the Philippine declaration of independence.
Travel by vehicle to Maragondon. Travel time depends on traffic.
See the trial house and follow the other side of the same revolution, the trial of the Bonifacio brothers.
Rest in town or visit a nearby attraction, then head back.
The two sites are some distance apart, so a vehicle is more convenient. With a private car, a rental, or a tour, you can combine them into one day.
Take a bus bound for Ternate or Maragondon from PITx (Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange) in Manila and get off in Maragondon. One blog describes this method.
Maragondon is about
54 km
from Manila and about
44 km
from the provincial capital, Imus. Travel time and fares depend on traffic and the bus company, so check at the terminal.
Tell the driver you are getting off in Maragondon town proper. The trial house is a few blocks from the town hall.
If you drive or rent a car, check parking around Col. C. Riel Street locally.
Tours that combine Cavite's historical sites sometimes appear, and the contents and prices vary by operator.
The museum is closed on Mondays, so be sure to check the day of the week before you travel.
The town is small and can be explored on foot, and a tricycle gets you to nearby spots quickly. Negotiate the fare before you ride.

Maragondon has a tropical climate. During the rainy months of June–October the roads can turn muddy, and bus service can be disrupted when a typhoon passes. The museum is indoors, so you can visit in the rain, but walking around town and getting there are less comfortable. The dry season from November to May is easier for getting around.

If you are interested in history, you could aim for around May 10, the execution anniversary, or around November 30, Bonifacio's birthday. The NHCP is known to hold wreath-laying and commemorative events. The schedule changes every year, so confirm before you go.

Maragondon is a small town with few places to stay, so many people make a day trip from Manila or from central Cavite. If you need a room, check accommodations in larger towns such as Imus or Cavite City on a booking site by date.
Eating at a local eatery in town and having Filipino home cooking is the realistic option. Shop names and hours change often, so check locally. Preparing water and snacks ahead makes the trip easier.

If you build a one- or two-day plan around Cavite's historical sites toward Imus and Kawit, it is easier to base yourself in a larger town such as Cavite City or Imus and travel from there. We suggest starting early, having lunch in Maragondon, and moving on to the next stop in the afternoon. At the market or small shops you can look at local snacks and bamboo crafts, but check items and prices locally.
The museum is closed on Mondays, and its opening hours (about 8–9 a.m. to 4–5 p.m.) and whether it opens on Sundays differ between sources, so check before you go.
Admission is listed as free, but this may change depending on circumstances.
The introductory video and the diorama are the key to understanding the course of the trial, so take your time with them first.
Walk carefully on the old stairs and floors of the house and do not touch them.
Ask the staff first whether photography is allowed and what the flash rules are.
If you would like an explanation, simply ask the staff. Schedules and formats may change.
The town is quiet, so look around during the daytime and head back early.
There is debate about how and where Bonifacio was executed, and markers and sources describe it differently. Do not settle on a single account; read the exhibits and other materials together.
Opening hours and closing days differ between sources, so check NHCP announcements just before your visit.
Bus frequency and travel times depend on traffic, so check your return transport in advance.
In the rainy season, typhoons or heavy rain can delay travel.
This is a historic site, so do not touch or damage exhibits or the building structure.
Take care of your valuables in town and keep your cash in separate places.

This is the setting of the Philippine declaration of independence in Kawit, and it lets you see the same revolutionary history from another angle. It is some distance from Maragondon, so a vehicle is more convenient.
This mountain lies inside the protected landscape that spans Maragondon and Ternate, and is worth considering as well if you enjoy hiking.
The provincial capital of Cavite, about
44 km
from Maragondon. It is a good transport hub.
The Our Lady of the Assumption Parish Church stands in town and is said to be reachable on foot together with the trial house.
